summary.en: Harvard, the oldest university in today's USA, is founded in 1636.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of a black-and-white historical copper engraving, not a historical image.

summary.en: The war of 1775–1783 in which thirteen British colonies in North America, with the support of France, Spain and the Netherlands, won their independence from Britain and became the USA. It was also a civil war between patriots and loyalists, and indigenous peoples and enslaved people were on both sides.

intro.en: The Seven Years' War ended in 1763 with France losing its possessions in North America, but Britain had incurred large debts. Parliament wanted the colonies to pay for their own defence and introduced new taxes and duties, such as the Stamp Act. Protests grew: the Boston Massacre in 1770, the Boston Tea Party in 1773 and the harsh laws against Massachusetts that followed in 1774. The colonies responded with a joint congress and a boycott of British goods. On 19 April 1775 British soldiers were to destroy the militia's weapons store in Concord, and the war broke out. On 4 July 1776 the colonies declared themselves independent. The war also divided the colonists: an estimated one fifth were loyalists who held fast to the Crown.

members.en: The thirteen colonies, from 1776 the USA, with the Continental Army under George Washington and the states' militias. France from 1778, Spain from 1779 (allied with France but not formally with the USA) and the Netherlands, against which Britain declared war in December 1780. Among the indigenous peoples, many Oneida and Tuscarora stood on the patriots' side. About 5,000 African Americans served in the Continental Army and the navy, and about 4,000 more in the militia and in other ways.

Britain, about 25,000 loyalists who fought for the Crown, about 30,000 hired soldiers from German states such as Hesse-Kassel, Hesse-Hanau and Brunswick, and about 13,000 warriors from indigenous peoples, among others the Seneca, Cayuga, Onondaga, part of the Mohawk, Cherokee and Muscogee. The British promised freedom to the enslaved people of patriots who went over to them (1775 and 1779). Estimates of how many served the British vary from 25,000 to 50,000.

outcome.en: After the defeat at Yorktown in 1781 the major fighting in North America ceased. In the Peace of Paris on 3 September 1783 Britain recognised the independence of the USA and handed over the land east of the Mississippi, south of the Great Lakes and north of Florida. In the peace treaties with France and Spain, France received Tobago and Senegal, and Spain received Menorca and Florida. The indigenous peoples were not part of the negotiations, and the fighting over the land in the west continued after the war. The British carried off 8,000–10,000 freed Black people from Charleston, Savannah and New York, while white loyalists took 15,000 enslaved people with them to Jamaica and the Bahamas. Many who had been promised freedom were returned to their owners.

casualties.en: How many died in total is largely unknown, and the figures are estimates. On the patriots' side more than 25,000 died in military service, of whom about 6,800 in battle and at least 17,000 of disease, many as prisoners of war. The British military lost 43,633 dead in 1775–1783 in all theatres (excluding officers), and about 7,774 German soldiers died in British service. France lost 2,112 killed in the USA and Spain 124 in West Florida. The losses among the indigenous peoples are unknown. A smallpox epidemic in North America in 1775–1782 killed an estimated 130,000 people.

summary.en: On 19 April 1775 British soldiers are to destroy the militia's weapons store in Concord. After a brief skirmish at Lexington, a day of fighting follows as the soldiers retreat to Boston, which the militia then besieges. These are the first battles of the war.

On 17 June 1775 the British take the Charlestown peninsula outside the besieged Boston. They win only on the third assault and suffer over 1,000 casualties, far more than the colonists. Most of the fighting took place on the neighbouring hill, Breed's Hill.

On 7 November 1775 Virginia's British governor, Lord Dunmore, promises freedom to enslaved people and servants of the patriots who enlist for the Crown. Between 800 and 2,000 enslaved people flee to him. The promise did not apply to the loyalists' enslaved people. In 1779 the British extended the offer to all colonies, and at least 20,000 enslaved people fled to British service during the war.

text.en: Wikidata's entry on the proclamation has no date or place, so the year and place could not be compared with a second, independent source. The information comes from Wikipedia.

summary.en: On 4 July 1776 the Second Continental Congress in Philadelphia adopts the Declaration of Independence, which was written almost entirely by Thomas Jefferson. The thirteen colonies declare themselves free from Britain. It is one of the first times that the colonies are called “United States”. Congress had voted for independence on 2 July.

caption.en: The US Declaration of Independence in William Stone's 1823 facsimile of the original document from 1776. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 6 August 1777, American militia and Oneida warriors walk into an ambush laid by Loyalists and Mohawk, Seneca, Cayuga, Onondaga and Mississauga warriors in British service. The battle is regarded as the start of a civil war within the Haudenosaunee (the Iroquois Confederacy), in which the Oneida and Tuscarora sided with the Patriots. In Haudenosaunee oral history, the place is called “a place of great sorrow”.

After two battles near Saratoga, on 19 September and 7 October 1777, the British general John Burgoyne surrenders on 17 October with about 6,200 soldiers. The victory convinces France that the United States can win, and in February 1778 France and the United States form an alliance.

text.en: Wikipedia gives the battles as 19 September and 7 October and the surrender as 17 October 1777. Wikidata gives the same start, but 17 December 1777 as the end.

summary.en: The British move the war to the South, where they count on support from Loyalists. After a siege of about six weeks, the American general Benjamin Lincoln surrenders on 12 May 1780, and over 5,000 soldiers are taken prisoner. It is one of the Patriots' worst defeats.

An American and French army under George Washington and Rochambeau surrounds the British general Cornwallis at Yorktown, while the French fleet under de Grasse closes the route by sea. On 19 October 1781 the British surrender, and more than 7,000 soldiers are taken prisoner. It is the last major land battle of the war, and it leads to peace negotiations.

On 3 September 1783 the peace treaty between Great Britain and the United States is signed in Paris. Great Britain recognises the independence of the United States, and the war is over. The United States receives the land east of the Mississippi, south of the Great Lakes and north of Florida, but the Indigenous peoples who lived there were not part of the negotiations.

text.en: One sentence in Wikipedia's article on the war says that the treaty was signed on 2 September and took effect from the following day. The article's introduction, the article on the peace treaty and Wikidata give 3 September 1783.

summary.en: Isaac Newton formulates his infinitesimal calculus in 1664–1666, during the isolation when the plague raged. Leibniz arrives at it independently around 1675.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of a watercoloured 17th-century copperplate engraving, not a historical image.

summary.en: From March to November 1584, Hashiba Hideyoshi, who later takes the name Toyotomi Hideyoshi, fights Oda Nobukatsu and Tokugawa Ieyasu in a series of battles around Komaki and Nagakute. Neither side wins decisively. The fighting ends when Nobukatsu makes peace with Hideyoshi in November, and Ieyasu then no longer has a reason to continue.

On 22 January 1517, the army of the Ottoman sultan Selim I defeats the Mamluks under Sultan Tumanbay II at their fortifications just outside Cairo. The Ottomans then take Cairo, and the Mamluk Sultanate comes to an end. The Ottoman grand vizier Hadım Sinan Pasha is killed in the battle.

text.en: Wikipedia and Wikidata give the same date but no coordinates, only that the battle took place just outside Cairo. The point comes from the Historical Conflict Event Dataset and is approximate.

summary.en: In October 1590 the Moroccan sultan Ahmad al-Mansur sends an army with cannon against the Songhai Empire. On 13 March 1591 it, under Judar Pasha, meets the Songhai army under Askia Ishaq II near Tondibi, north of the capital Gao. The Moroccans win, and the Songhai Empire collapses.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 13 March 1591 and Wikidata 12 March 1591. Neither has coordinates, so the point comes from the Historical Conflict Event Dataset and is approximate.

summary.en: On 27 February 1776, North Carolina militia defeat reinforcements for the British governor Josiah Martin at a bridge near Wilmington. The battle is small but becomes a turning point in the war, less than five months before the Declaration of Independence.
On 8 September 1781, American and British troops meet at Eutaw Springs. It is the last major battle of the war in the Carolinas, and both sides afterwards claim to have won.

During the Scanian War, the armies of Sweden and Denmark meet on Yllesheds heath outside Landskrona on 14 July 1677. The Swedish army, reinforced with 4,000 peasants from Småland, had marched south to attack the Danes before reinforcements could arrive. Sweden wins.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 14 July 1677. Wikidata gives two dates, 14 and 24 July 1677. The ten-day difference is probably because the date has been reckoned in different calendars (Julian and Gregorian). We show the date as Wikipedia writes it.

summary.en: Miguel de Cervantes, the author of Don Quixote and one of the greatest writers in Spanish, dies in Madrid on 22 April 1616.

caption.en: Portrait of Miguel de Cervantes, attributed to Juan de Jáuregui, around 1600. According to the file page, current scholarship does not consider any portrait of Cervantes to be authentic. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: William Shakespeare dies on 23 April 1616 in Stratford-upon-Avon, where he was also born. He is regarded as the greatest writer in English.

text.en: Shakespeare died on 23 April 1616 according to the Julian calendar that England used at the time. According to the Gregorian calendar, which Catholic countries had introduced in 1582, it was 3 May.

caption.en: William Shakespeare in the Chandos portrait, attributed to John Taylor, in the National Portrait Gallery in London. It is one of few portraits that may have been painted during his lifetime. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Tokugawa Ieyasu, who founded the Tokugawa shogunate in Japan, dies at Sunpu Castle on 1 June 1616.

text.en: Ieyasu died on the 17th day of the fourth month in the year Genna 2 according to the Japanese calendar. This corresponds to 1 June 1616 in the Western calendar.

caption.en: Portrait of Tokugawa Ieyasu, painted by Kanō Tan'yū in the early Edo period. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Enslaved Africans in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose up in 1791. It became the start of thirteen years of war, in which Spain and Britain also became involved. The revolution ended with Haiti becoming independent in 1804, the only state to have been founded after a successful slave revolt.

text.en: Wikipedia counts the start of the revolution from the uprising on the night of 22 August 1791. Wikidata gives both 14 August (the meeting where the uprising was planned) and 22 August. The end, the declaration of independence on 1 January 1804, is the same in both.

intro.en: Saint-Domingue was France's most profitable colony. Its wealth came from sugar, coffee and indigo plantations where enslaved Africans worked under very harsh conditions, and many died soon after being brought there. The enslaved outnumbered the white colonists and the free people of colour combined by about ten to one. The French Revolution and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen in 1789 raised the question of whom freedom applied to. Free people of colour demanded citizenship rights, and the white plantation owners refused. On the night of 22 August 1791, the enslaved on the northern plain rose up.

name.en: The insurgents, later the Haitian army

members.en: The enslaved people who rose up in 1791, at first under leaders such as Dutty Boukman, Jean-François Papillon and Georges Biassou, later under Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines. Until 1794 many fought on the Spanish side; Toussaint went over to France in May 1794, after France had abolished slavery. From October 1802, Dessalines and Alexandre Pétion fought against France, and in 1803 Britain blockaded the French ports.

France (the monarchy, then the republic and finally Napoleon Bonaparte as First Consul) and the white colonists. Spain (1793–1795) and Britain (1793–1798) entered the colony during the war against revolutionary France and tried to take it for themselves. Napoleon's army, which arrived in 1802, had secret instructions to reintroduce slavery, at least in the former Spanish part of the island.

outcome.en: The last French troops left the colony at the end of 1803, and on 1 January 1804 Dessalines declared Haiti independent. Haiti became the first independent state in Latin America and the first led by formerly enslaved people. From February to April 1804, between 3,000 and 5,000 of the remaining white people were killed on Dessalines' orders. France recognised Haiti's independence only in 1825, in return for an indemnity of 150 million francs that became a heavy burden for the country. The revolution influenced the debate on slavery throughout the Americas.

casualties.en: Estimates differ widely. According to most accounts, about 200,000 Haitians died, but the historian Robert Scheina has estimated 350,000. France lost 57,000–75,000 dead, and British losses are given as about 100,000 dead or wounded. About 25,000 white colonists died. Most of the European soldiers died of yellow fever, while most Haitians were killed by violence. The figures are estimates.

text.en: The revolution is one of the only known slave revolts in history that led to the founding of a state. It influenced views on slavery throughout the Americas and strengthened the struggle to abolish it.
The indemnity to France drained Haiti's treasury and gave the country a long period of instability. The debt was not paid off until 1947.

Historians still disagree about how much the revolution mattered. David Geggus argues that it made limited difference, since slavery remained in the Americas for many decades more. W. E. B. Du Bois saw it as an economic pressure, without which the British Parliament would not have backed abolitionism, the movement against slavery.
No one knows for certain how many died. Most accounts say about 200,000 Haitians, but other estimates are higher.

summary.en: On the night between 21 and 22 August 1791, the enslaved people on the plantations of northern Saint-Domingue rise up. Within a few weeks tens of thousands have joined, and plantation after plantation is burned. The uprising becomes the start of the Haitian Revolution.

text.en: According to tradition, the uprising was set off at a Vodou ceremony in the forest of Bois Caïman, led by Dutty Boukman and Cécile Fatiman. There are no eyewitness accounts, and the sources give different dates (14, 21 or 24 August). Some historians doubt that the ceremony took place as it is told.

summary.en: On 29 August 1793, the French commissioner Léger-Félicité Sonthonax declares all enslaved people in the colony's northern province free, in order to win them over to the French side against Spain and Britain. The commissioner Étienne Polverel does the same in the rest of the colony on 31 October. On 4 February 1794, the National Convention in Paris abolishes slavery in all French colonies.

text.en: Wikipedia's articles on the law of 4 February 1794 and on Napoleon's expedition give 29 August 1793. One section of Wikipedia's article on the revolution says 1792, but the same article gives 1793 in another place.

summary.en: Construction of the Taj Mahal in Agra, a tomb monument for Mumtaz Mahal, begins in 1632. The whole complex is believed to have been completed in 1653.

text.en: Wikipedia states that construction began in 1632 and that the whole complex was completed in 1653. World History Encyclopedia also gives 1632 as the start, but 1649 as the year the Taj Mahal was completed.

caption.en: The Taj Mahal in Agra with the garden in front. Photochrom (a colour-printed image after a photograph) from Photoglob Co. in Zurich, around 1890–1910. The Library of Congress states no known restrictions on publication.

summary.en: Violent conflicts between Australia's Indigenous peoples and mainly British settlers, soldiers and police, from the first months after the British colony was founded in 1788 until at least 1928, in some places until 1934. The fighting was local and scattered across the whole continent, often in the form of raids and massacres rather than battles. The number of dead is disputed, but tens of thousands of Aboriginal people were killed.

text.en: Wikipedia describes the frontier wars as lasting from 1788 to at least 1928, with isolated conflicts as late as 1934. Wikidata instead gives September 1794 to 1899. The war has no clear beginning or end, and for a long time it was not even called a war: in 1968 the anthropologist W. E. H. Stanner spoke of “the great Australian silence” about Indigenous resistance in historical writing.

intro.en: In January 1788, Britain founded a penal colony at Sydney Cove, on the land of the Eora people. The governor had orders to live in friendship with the Indigenous peoples, but when the colonists cleared land, fished and grazed their cattle on their hunting grounds and watering places, fighting broke out. The pattern was repeated for 150 years as the colonies grew: settlers, gold diggers and cattle owners took land, and the Indigenous peoples resisted with raids, attacks on cattle and sometimes open battles. The colonists often responded with punitive expeditions and massacres. On top of this came diseases such as smallpox, and according to the historian Geoffrey Blainey, disease was the greatest conqueror.

members.en: Many different peoples who mostly resisted separately, among them the Bidjigal and Darug under Pemulwuy around Sydney, the Wiradjuri under Windradyne, the Noongar under Yagan in Western Australia, the peoples of Tasmania, the Kamilaroi, Gunditjmara, Kalkadoon in Queensland, the Bunuba under Jandamarra, the Warlpiri and the Yolngu. Not all resisted, and many Indigenous men served in the mounted police.
British soldiers, settlers, convicts and stockmen, colonial police and mounted police, and in Queensland the special force Native Police, with officers drawn from the Indigenous peoples.

outcome.en: The colonists took land across the whole continent. The Indigenous population fell from an estimated 300,000 to 3 million in 1788 to about 90,000 in 1901, through disease, starvation, displacement and violence. In Victoria, the Yoorrook Commission concluded that British policy amounted to genocide. The frontier wars have long been absent from the Australian War Memorial in Canberra, but in 2022 its leadership promised a broader account of the violence against Indigenous peoples.

casualties.en: Estimates differ widely. The Colonial Frontier Massacres project (Lyndall Ryan) counts 11,000–14,000 killed in massacres with at least six victims. Henry Reynolds estimated over 30,000 dead in 2022. Robert Ørsted-Jensen and Raymond Evans argue that at least 100,000 Indigenous people were killed, about 65,000 of them in Queensland, but other researchers have criticised their method. Among the colonists and their helpers, the death toll has been estimated at 2,000–2,500.

summary.en: The Bidjigal warrior Pemulwuy, of the Darug people, has been leading a guerrilla war against the colonists since 1790. In March 1797, he and up to 100 warriors meet armed settlers and soldiers at Parramatta. Pemulwuy is hit by seven bullets and taken prisoner, but recovers and escapes. He was killed in 1802.

text.en: Wikipedia gives the end of March 1797 without a day. Wikidata gives 22 March 1797.

summary.en: Wars between Hawaiian chiefs (aliʻi) for power over the Hawaiian Islands in 1782–1810. Kamehameha, who in Hawaiian is called Ka Naʻi aupuni, “the one who unified the kingdom”, first conquered the island of Hawaiʻi and then Maui, Molokaʻi and Oʻahu, and in 1810 the king of Kauaʻi submitted. The islands thereby became a unified kingdom.

text.en: The information is based on Wikipedia, and Wikidata has no entry of its own for the war, only for the battles. Wikipedia says in one place that Kamehameha began his campaign in 1783, but his first major victory, at Mokuʻōhai, was in 1782. For the invasion of 1795, the article on the Battle of Nuʻuanu gives about 12,000 men and 1,200 war canoes, while the article on Kamehameha gives 10,000 men and 960 canoes.

intro.en: When Kalaniʻōpuʻu, ruler (aliʻi nui) of the island of Hawaiʻi, died in 1782, the kingdom was inherited by his son Kīwalaʻō. His nephew Kamehameha was instead given a religious task, to tend the war god Kūkaʻilimoku, and the valley of Waipiʻo. When chiefs from Kona chose to support Kamehameha, war broke out. The other islands were ruled by their own chiefs, chiefly Kahekili II on Maui and Oʻahu. During the war Kamehameha bought guns and ammunition from British and American traders, and the Britons John Young and Isaac Davis became his advisers.

members.en: Kamehameha and his relatives and allies among the chiefs of Kona, among them Keʻeaumoku, Keaweaheulu, Kekūhaupiʻo and the twins Kameʻeiamoku and Kamanawa, with the advisers John Young and Isaac Davis.

On the island of Hawaiʻi, Kīwalaʻō and later his half-brother Keōua Kūʻahuʻula; on Maui, Molokaʻi and Oʻahu, Kahekili II and his son Kalanikūpule, who in 1795 was helped by the chief Kaʻiana when he went over from Kamehameha; on Kauaʻi, Kāʻeokūlani and then Kaumualiʻi.

outcome.en: After the victory at Nuʻuanu in 1795, Kamehameha's realm was for the first time called the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi. Two attempts to conquer Kauaʻi failed, in 1796 because of a storm and in 1803 because of disease, but in 1810 Kauaʻi's king Kaumualiʻi recognised Kamehameha as supreme ruler and was allowed to keep governing the island under him. Kamehameha gave the kingdom a common legal system.

casualties.en: The sources have no overall estimates of how many died. At Kepaniwai in 1790 so many died that, according to tradition, the stream was “dammed up” by the dead, and at Nuʻuanu in 1795 over 700 Oʻahu warriors fell or were pushed over the Nuʻuanu Pali cliff. When a road was built there in 1898, 800 skulls were found.

summary.en: Kamehameha and the chiefs from Kona defeat Kīwalaʻō, who is killed in the battle. Women and children from both sides seek shelter at the place of refuge Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau. After the victory, Kamehameha rules the northern and western parts of the island of Hawaiʻi.

text.en: Wikipedia gives only the year 1782. Wikidata gives July 1782.

summary.en: Kamehameha's army of about 1,200 warriors lands on Maui and meets Kalanikūpule's forces in ʻĪao Valley. After two days of evenly matched fighting, two cannon, operated by John Young and Isaac Davis, decide the outcome. The battle is among the bloodiest in Hawaiian history, and the name Kepaniwai means roughly “the dammed waters”.

In the summer of 1791, Kamehameha's great temple Puʻukoholā Heiau is completed. He invites his cousin and rival Keōua Kūʻahuʻula there, seemingly for peace negotiations. When Keōua steps ashore, he and his entourage are killed. Kamehameha now rules the whole island of Hawaiʻi.

text.en: The event is based only on Wikipedia (the articles on Kamehameha I and Puʻukoholā Heiau). The sources give different versions of how Keōua died.

summary.en: In May 1795, Kamehameha's army lands at Waikīkī and drives Kalanikūpule's forces up Nuʻuanu Valley. At the Nuʻuanu Pali cliff, over 700 Oʻahu warriors fall or are pushed over the precipice. In Hawaiian the battle is called Kalelekaʻanae, “the leaping mullet”. After the victory, Kamehameha's realm is for the first time called the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi.

text.en: Wikipedia and Wikidata both give May 1795 and Nuʻuanu, but the coordinates differ: Wikipedia gives a point at 21.233° N, south of the valley, while Wikidata gives 21.367° N at Nuʻuanu Pali. The globe uses Wikidata's point. Wikipedia also points out that there are “varying and sometimes conflicting” accounts of the battle.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of an engraving from a Pacific voyage, not a historical image.

summary.en: One of the most devastating wars in the history of Europe, fought mainly in Central Europe. An estimated 4.5–8 million soldiers and civilians died of fighting, starvation or disease.

intro.en: The Reformation had divided the Holy Roman Empire between Catholics and Protestants. The Peace of Augsburg in 1555 was meant to keep them apart, but it did not hold as Protestantism spread. The war broke out in 1618, when the Protestant Frederick V of the Palatinate became king of Bohemia instead of the Catholic Ferdinand II. What began as a conflict within the empire became a European war: Denmark and Sweden entered to win land and protect the Protestants, and from 1635 France fought against its rivals the Habsburgs.

members.en: Bohemia, the Palatinate, Denmark–Norway, Sweden, the Netherlands, Hesse-Kassel and others, and from 1635 France. Saxony and Brandenburg were on this side until the Peace of Prague in 1635.
The Emperor and the Habsburg monarchy, Spain, Bavaria and the Catholic League.

outcome.en: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648. The states of the empire, such as Bavaria and Saxony, gained greater independence. Sweden gained land in northern Germany, including Western Pomerania, Wismar and Bremen-Verden. France gained the Decapolis and Sundgau, and Spain recognised the independence of the Netherlands.

casualties.en: About 4.5–8 million soldiers and civilians died of fighting, starvation and disease, of whom 1.3–1.8 million were soldiers. In places in Germany the population fell by more than half. The figures are estimates and are given as ranges.

caption.en: The Defenestration of Prague in 1618, when the war began. Copper engraving by Matthäus Merian in the chronicle Theatrum Europaeum (volume 1, 1662 edition). Public domain.

summary.en: On 23 May 1618, representatives of the Emperor are thrown out of a window in Prague. The event marks the start of the war.
The battle on 8 November 1620 near Prague belongs to the Bohemian Revolt, the first phase of the war.
On 17 September 1631, Gustavus Adolphus leads Swedish and Saxon troops to victory over the armies of the Emperor and the Catholic League.
On 16 November 1632, Swedish and Imperial armies meet at Lützen. Gustavus Adolphus is killed during the battle.

caption.en: The death of Gustavus Adolphus at Lützen. Painting by Carl Wahlbom, 1855. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 5–6 September 1634, Imperial and Spanish troops defeat the Swedes and their German allies.
On 4 October 1636, a Swedish army under Johan Banér wins a battle at Wittstock.
On 19 May 1643, French troops defeat a Spanish army at Rocroi.
On 6 March 1645, Sweden wins a battle at Jankov in Bohemia.
The peace treaties in Osnabrück and Münster are signed on 24 October 1648 and end the war.

A war over power around the Baltic Sea in 1700–1721. A coalition led by Russia broke Sweden's position as a great power, and Russia became the leading power in the region. Probably more than a million people died.

text.en: The sources give dates in three different calendars: the Julian (Old Style), the Gregorian (New Style) and the Swedish. Sweden skipped the leap day in 1700 and had its own Swedish calendar from 1 March 1700 to 30 February 1712, one day ahead of the Julian and ten days behind the Gregorian. Sweden then returned to the Julian calendar and did not switch to the Gregorian until 1753. The Battle of Poltava is therefore given as 27 June (Julian), 28 June (Swedish) or 8 July 1709 (Gregorian). On the globe, all dates are given in the Gregorian calendar.

intro.en: Between 1560 and 1658, Sweden built up an empire around the Baltic Sea, with Karelia, Ingria, Estonia and Livonia, and after the Thirty Years' War also land in northern Germany. When the young Charles XII became king, the neighbours saw a chance to take land from Sweden. Tsar Peter I of Russia, Frederick IV of Denmark–Norway and Augustus II, Elector of Saxony and King of Poland–Lithuania, formed an alliance against Sweden in 1699. In 1700 Denmark attacked Sweden's ally Holstein-Gottorp, Saxony attacked Livonia and besieged Riga, and Russia entered Ingria.

members.en: Sweden and Holstein-Gottorp, Polish nobles under Stanisław I (1705–1709) and Cossacks under hetman Ivan Mazepa (1708–1714). The Ottoman Empire received Charles XII at Bender and in 1710–1713 went to war against Russia.

Russia, Denmark–Norway (1700 and 1709–1720), Saxony and Poland–Lithuania under Augustus II (until 1706 and from 1709), Prussia (1715–1720) and Hanover (1715–1719), with the support of Britain (1715–1719).

outcome.en: Sweden lost. Peace was concluded in several treaties: with Hanover and Prussia in Stockholm in 1719–1720, with Denmark–Norway at Frederiksborg in 1720 and with Russia at Nystad in 1721. Russia gained Estonia, Livonia, Ingria and parts of Karelia, while Finland was returned to Sweden. Prussia gained part of Swedish Pomerania with the mouth of the Oder, Hanover gained Bremen-Verden and Denmark strengthened its position in Schleswig. Russia became the leading power around the Baltic Sea. In Sweden, absolutism ended after the death of Charles XII, and the Age of Liberty began.

casualties.en: Probably more than a million people died. Sweden lost at least 200,000 soldiers, and including civilians Sweden with its possessions is estimated to have lost about 350,000 of 2.5 million inhabitants. On the coalition's side at least 400,000 soldiers died, of whom about 300,000 in the Russian army. The population of Poland–Lithuania fell from 8 to 6.5 million up to 1720. The figures are estimates and differ between researchers.

summary.en: On 22 February 1700, Saxon troops in the service of Augustus II besiege Riga in Swedish Livonia. The Swedish garrison under Erik Dahlberg holds the city. The sources give the same day as the start of the war.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 12 February 1700 in the Julian calendar and 22 February in the Gregorian. Wikidata gives 22 February (Gregorian).

summary.en: On 30 November 1700, a Swedish relief army under Charles XII defeats the Russian army besieging Narva, even though the Russians outnumber them three or four to one.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 19 November (Julian calendar), 20 November (Swedish calendar) and 30 November 1700 (Gregorian). Wikidata gives 30 November (Gregorian).

summary.en: On 8 July 1709, a Russian army under Tsar Peter I defeats the Swedish army at Poltava. It is the largest and most decisive battle of the war, and it becomes the beginning of the end for Sweden as a great power.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 27 June (Julian calendar), 28 June (Swedish calendar) and 8 July 1709 (Gregorian). Wikidata gives the same date in the Julian and Gregorian calendars.

caption.en: The Battle of Poltava in a painting by Pierre-Denis Martin, 1726, in the Catherine Palace. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 11 July 1709, three days after Poltava, almost the entire Swedish army surrenders at the Dnieper river. Charles XII has already crossed the river and flees to Moldavia, a vassal state under the Ottoman Empire.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 30 June (Julian calendar), 1 July (Swedish calendar) and 11 July 1709 (Gregorian). Wikidata gives 1 July 1709 but marks it as the Julian calendar, which would correspond to 12 July. The year and place agree, but not the day.

summary.en: On 10 March 1710, a Swedish army under Magnus Stenbock defeats an equally large Danish army outside Helsingborg. Denmark's attempt to retake Scania fails, and it becomes the last major battle of the war on Swedish soil.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 27 February (Julian calendar), 28 February (Swedish calendar) and 10 March 1710 (Gregorian). Wikidata gives 10 March (Gregorian).

summary.en: On 20 December 1712, Swedish troops under Magnus Stenbock defeat a Danish and Saxon army in Mecklenburg. It becomes Sweden's last major victory in the war.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 9 December (Julian calendar, to which Sweden had by then returned) and 20 December 1712 (Gregorian). Wikidata gives 20 December (Gregorian).

summary.en: On 7 August 1714, the Russian fleet defeats Swedish ships at Hanko Peninsula. It is the Russian fleet's first important victory, and afterwards Russia takes Åland.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 27 July (Julian calendar) and 7 August 1714 (Gregorian). Wikidata gives 26 July 1714 (Julian), that is, one day earlier. The year and place agree, but not the day.

summary.en: During the siege of the Norwegian fortress of Fredriksten, Charles XII is hit in the head by a projectile, probably a bullet, and dies on 11 December 1718. The Swedes call off the attack on Norway, and his death marks the end of absolutism in Sweden.

text.en: Wikipedia states that Charles XII died on 30 November 1718 in the Julian calendar (which Sweden then used), which is 11 December in the Gregorian. Wikidata gives 30 November 1718 but marks it as the Gregorian calendar. The year and place agree, but not the calendar.

summary.en: Russia and Sweden make peace at Nystad on 10 September 1721, ending the war. Sweden cedes Estonia, Livonia, Ingria and parts of Karelia to Russia, and Finland is returned to Sweden.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 30 August (Julian calendar) and 10 September 1721 (Gregorian). Wikidata gives 30 August (Julian), the same day.

summary.en: The Portuguese governor Afonso de Albuquerque takes the city of Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate, with the support of Timoji and his troops. He first took the city in February 1510 but was driven out by the sultan Ismail Adil Shah in May; on 25 November the city is stormed again. The soldiers are allowed to plunder it for four days, and the Muslims who have not fled are killed on the governor's orders. Goa becomes the capital of Portuguese India and remains Portuguese for over 450 years, until India takes the territory in December 1961.

The governor of the Dutch East India Company, Jan Pieterszoon Coen, returns with reinforcements on 28 May 1619 and two days later has the city of Jayakarta razed to the ground and its inhabitants driven away. On the ruins a fort and a city are built, which are named Batavia in 1621. It becomes the centre of the Company's trade in Asia and then the capital of the Dutch East Indies. Batavia remains a European colonial city for about 320 years, until Japan occupies it in 1942. In independent Indonesia the city is called Jakarta.

caption.en: The founding of Batavia as Barend Wijnveld painted it in the 19th century, not an image from 1619. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In 1652 an expedition from the Dutch East India Company under Jan van Riebeeck founds a station at the Cape of Good Hope, where the company's ships travelling between the Netherlands and Batavia can obtain fresh supplies. It becomes Cape Town and the beginning of the Cape Colony. The land at the foot of Table Mountain was the grazing ground of the Khoikhoi, and when the settlers took it, the first of the wars between the Khoikhoi and the Dutch began. War and smallpox, including in 1713 and 1755, then broke down Khoikhoi societies, and they were driven out beyond the borders of the colony.

The Virginia Company of London founds James Fort on the James River on 14 May 1607 (4 May according to the old calendar). It becomes the first lasting English settlement in America. The island they chose was used by the Paspahegh people, and only 60 of the first 214 settlers survived the starving winter of 1609–1610. Relations with the Powhatan soon turned into war. In August 1619 the first documented enslaved Africans arrived in the colony, and in 1622 the indigenous people struck back in an uprising that devastated the settlements around Jamestown.

caption.en: The English arrival at Jamestown in 1607, illustration from a book of 1919, not an image from the time of the event. Licence: CC0.

summary.en: Between 1545 and 1548 the highlands of Mexico are struck by an epidemic with high fever and bleeding, which the Aztecs call cocoliztli, “plague” in Nahuatl. An estimated 5–15 million people die, up to 80 per cent of the indigenous population, including about 800,000 in the Valley of Mexico. It is one of the worst population catastrophes in history. The indigenous population is hit hardest, because after the conquest it had been forced together into new villages, weakened by war and forced labour, and the epidemic comes during a long period of severe drought. The shortage of labour leads to famine, and the Spaniards seize the land left behind by the dead.

text.en: Nobody knows for certain. Researchers have proposed a native virus-caused haemorrhagic fever spread by rodents and made worse by the drought, while DNA analyses in 2018 of skeletons from Oaxaca found the bacterium Salmonella Paratyphi C, which causes paratyphoid fever. Other researchers argue that the symptoms do not match paratyphoid. The death tolls are estimates with great uncertainty.

summary.en: In 1576 a new great cocoliztli epidemic comes, after a drought that stretched from Venezuela to Canada. About 2–2.5 million people die, roughly half of the indigenous population that remained after the epidemic of 1545–1548. The physician Francisco Hernández sees the disease at close quarters and describes high fever, severe headache, black tongue, jaundice and heavy bleeding. After the epidemic the Spaniards decide in 1577 that the tax from the indigenous peoples may be paid only in maize and money. The population of Mexico did not reach the same level as before the conquest until the 20th century.

text.en: Wikipedia says the epidemic lasted until about 1580 and killed about two million. The article by Acuna-Soto and others (2002) gives 1576–1578 and 2–2.5 million dead. Which disease it was is as uncertain as for the epidemic of 1545.

summary.en: On 20 November 1542 Emperor Charles V issues the New Laws. Since 1502 Spanish colonists in America had been able to obtain the right to demand labour and tribute from groups of indigenous inhabitants, the encomienda, a system that in practice became a kind of slavery. The Laws of Burgos of 1512 were meant to regulate the work but were poorly followed. After protests from, among others, the Dominican Bartolomé de las Casas, the New Laws now forbid indigenous people to be made slaves, and the encomienda is to be phased out by no longer being allowed to be inherited. The colonists resist: in Peru the viceroy Blasco Núñez Vela is killed in 1546 by encomenderos under Gonzalo Pizarro, and in Mexico the viceroy refrains from carrying out the laws. Parts of the laws are withdrawn in 1545, but thousands of workers are freed.

caption.en: The title page of the 1543 printing of the New Laws. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The viceroy Francisco de Toledo turns the labour obligation of the Inca Empire, mit'a, into forced labour for Spain's silver mines on the mountain Cerro Rico. The first workers arrive in Potosí in 1573. The villages in an area of almost 520,000 square kilometres, from southern Peru through present-day Bolivia, must send every seventh adult man, about 13,000 men a year. They carry ore in sacks of 45–135 kilograms up ladders in narrow shafts, and many die in accidents, of pneumonia and of mercury poisoning. Thousands flee their villages to escape. By the end of the 17th century Upper Peru has lost almost half of its indigenous population compared with a little over a hundred years earlier.

text.en: Wikipedia on mit'a and on Potosí states that the first workers came in 1573, while the article on Cerro Rico says that Toledo introduced mit'a in 1574. How many died in the mines is very uncertain: one estimate is eight million, but other sources speak of hundreds of thousands and argue that eight million refers to the whole Viceroyalty of Peru.

summary.en: About 16 months after the British colony was founded, an epidemic breaks out among the indigenous peoples around Port Jackson. It probably began in March 1789 and died down in early May. In April the British notice that the canoes have disappeared from the bay, and they find sick and dead people in the rock crevices. Both the governor Arthur Phillip and the Eora man Bennelong believed that about half of the Eora people in the Sydney area died. Arabanoo, who lived in the colony and cared for the sick, also died. None of the British colonists appears to have fallen ill, but a sailor from North America died. The historian Peter Dowling argues that the epidemic probably made it impossible for the indigenous peoples to drive the colony away during its first years.

text.en: Most historians call the disease smallpox, as the colonists themselves did. Some physicians and researchers argue that it may have been chickenpox, to which the British were immune but the indigenous peoples were not. How the disease reached Sydney, and how many died, is still debated.

summary.en: On 31 October 1517 Martin Luther sends his 95 Theses to Archbishop Albrecht of Brandenburg. The theses criticise the trade in indulgences and how it relates to repentance, penance and the power of the pope. According to tradition Luther also nailed them to the door of the All Saints' Church in Wittenberg, but this is disputed. In retrospect the theses are regarded as the beginning of the Protestant Reformation.

caption.en: The first page of the 95 Theses in a printed edition from Basel, 1517. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 10 August 1519 Ferdinand Magellan's fleet leaves Seville, and on 20 September the five ships with about 270 men sail out from Sanlúcar de Barrameda. Magellan is killed in battle on Mactan in the Philippines in April 1521. In September 1522 the ship Victoria under Juan Sebastián Elcano returns to Spain with only 18 of the 270 men. It is the first voyage around the world.

caption.en: Magellan's voyage in an allegorical image by Johannes Stradanus from about 1592. A later image. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus's book De revolutionibus orbium coelestium is printed in Nuremberg, shortly before his death the same year. The book puts forward a model in which the Sun stands in the centre and the Earth is one of the planets orbiting it. The transition to that view of the world helped to start the Scientific Revolution.

caption.en: Copernicus's image of the solar system with the Sun in the centre, from De revolutionibus (1543). Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 13 March 1610 Galileo Galilei publishes Sidereus Nuncius (The Starry Messenger) in the Republic of Venice. In it he describes what he has seen through his telescope: that the surface of the Moon is uneven and mountainous, that the Milky Way consists of hundreds of stars not visible to the naked eye, and that celestial bodies orbit Jupiter. It is the first scientific work based on observations through a telescope.

caption.en: Two drawings of the Moon with shadows and craters, from Galileo's Sidereus nuncius. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

summary.en: In July 1687 Isaac Newton's book Principia is published. It sets out Newton's laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation and becomes the mathematical foundation of classical mechanics. Edmond Halley paid for the publication at his own risk, because the Royal Society had used up its money on books. The book is regarded as one of the most important works in the history of science.

caption.en: The title page of the first edition of Newton's Principia, 1687. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In April 1770 James Cook and the crew of HMS Endeavour sight the east coast of Australia. On 29 April they go ashore for the first time, at Botany Bay, where two men of the Gweagal people come down to the boat. Cook then follows the coast northwards and in August 1770 claims the whole east coast for Great Britain, on an island that he calls Possession Island.

caption.en: People in a canoe in Botany Bay, drawn by Tupaia, who travelled with Cook, in April 1770. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 13 May 1787 eleven British ships with about 1,420 people leave Portsmouth under Captain Arthur Phillip. They reach Botany Bay on 18 January 1788, but Phillip rejects the site. On 26 January the fleet anchors in Sydney Cove and raises the British flag. There the colony of New South Wales is founded as a penal colony, the beginning of British settlement in Australia. Conflicts soon arise, and the Eora people and Pemulwuy of the Bidjigal clan resist the colonists.

caption.en: The First Fleet sailing into Port Jackson on 27 January 1788. Wash drawing by William Bradley, who was on board, from his journal of about 1802. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 14 July 1789 the Bastille in Paris is stormed, a medieval fortress used as an arsenal and political prison. There are only seven prisoners there. The fortress's governor de Launay is killed after surrendering. The fall of the Bastille becomes the starting signal of the French Revolution, and 14 July is today France's national day.

caption.en: The storming of the Bastille, painting by an unknown artist in the collections of Versailles. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 14 May 1796 Edward Jenner tests his idea: he inoculates pus from cowpox blisters on the milkmaid Sarah Nelmes into James Phipps, the son of his gardener. When Phipps is later exposed to smallpox he does not fall ill. Jenner develops the smallpox vaccine, the world's first vaccine, and is often called the father of immunology.

caption.en: Edward Jenner. Mezzotint by John Raphael Smith from 1800. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

summary.en: For more than 300 years enslaved Africans were carried by ship across the Atlantic to the Americas. The first known direct voyage from Africa took place in 1519, and the last known slave ship to Cuba arrived in 1867. Most came from West and Central Africa and were forced to work on plantations, in mines and in households. According to current estimates about 12.75 million people were loaded onto slave ships, and up to 2 million of them died during the voyage. Portugal, Britain, Spain and France were among the largest slave-trading nations.

With a series of edicts between 1633 and 1639 the Tokugawa shogunate greatly restricted Japan's contacts with the outside world. Almost all foreigners were forbidden to enter the country, and ordinary Japanese were not allowed to travel abroad. Trade nevertheless remained, including with China at Nagasaki and with the Dutch on the island of Dejima, the only European trading post. The policy ended after 1853, when an American fleet under Matthew Perry forced Japan to open up to trade.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the policy was introduced in 1633–1639 and ended after 1853. Wikidata gives 1639–1854 (when the Convention of Kanagawa was concluded).

summary.en: James Watt worked as an instrument maker at the University of Glasgow and saw that Newcomen's steam engine wasted energy because the cylinder was cooled and reheated at every stroke. In May 1765, during a walk across Glasgow Green, he got the idea of letting the steam condense in a separate chamber, a condenser, so that the cylinder could be kept hot. He received a patent for the invention in 1769. The first engines with Watt's design were put into use in businesses in 1776 and were first used to pump water out of mines. The improvement made the steam engine much more efficient and was of great importance for the Industrial Revolution.

On 6 March 1521 Magellan's Spanish expedition reached the Marianas and anchored at Guam, after three months and twenty days across the Pacific. It was the first known contact between Europeans and the Chamorro people. Chamorros came out in fast outrigger canoes and took objects from the ships, especially anything made of iron; according to one historian they had a different view of ownership than the sailors, and Magellan called the island the Island of Thieves. After a clash in which at least one Chamorro was killed, Magellan had 40–50 houses burned and seven men killed, and on 9 March the fleet sailed on. The landing place is traditionally given as Umatac, but it may have been Tumon.

The Spanish navigator Álvaro de Mendaña left Callao in Peru in November 1567 with two ships and about 150 people. On 7 February 1568 the expedition sighted Santa Isabel and landed there a few days later, as the first known Europeans in the Solomon Islands; the islands received the name Islas Salomon after the return home. The Spaniards also explored, among other places, Malaita, Guadalcanal and Makira. When they tried to trade for food, the encounters with the islanders time and again went from friendly reception to misunderstandings, thefts and violent reprisals. In August 1568 they decided to turn back to Peru.

In May 1606 Pedro Fernandes de Queirós, a Portuguese navigator in Spanish service, reached the islands that are today Vanuatu. He landed on a large island that he believed was part of the sought-after southern continent and called it Austrialia del Espíritu Santo; the island is still called Espiritu Santo. Queirós wanted to found a colony there, Nova Jerusalem, but within a few weeks the plan was abandoned because of the hostility of the ni-Vanuatu and disagreement among the crew. After six weeks the ships sailed away from there.

On 26 February 1606 the Dutchman Willem Janszoon and the crew of the ship Duyfken landed at the Pennefather River on the Cape York Peninsula. It is the first known European landing in Australia. Janszoon charted about 320 kilometres of coast, which he believed was part of New Guinea, and turned back at a cape that he called Kaap Keerweer. The meeting with the Aboriginal people became violent: nine of the crew were killed during the voyage, but where and when is unclear, and some Aboriginal oral traditions place all nine deaths at Kaap Keerweer.

text.en: Where the nine sailors were killed is disputed. The historian Miriam Estensen argues that eight died on the island of Yos Sudarso near New Guinea and one on the Australian coast. The Dutch Australian Cultural Centre, which also builds on accounts from Aboriginal elders, argues that three died at Kaap Keerweer and five at Yos Sudarso on the way home. Some Aboriginal oral traditions place all nine at Kaap Keerweer.

summary.en: After Luís Vaz de Torres was separated from Queirós at Espiritu Santo, he sailed towards Manila at the end of June 1606. He followed the south coast of New Guinea, where the Spaniards came into sometimes violent contact with the local population and took twenty people captive. He then made his way through the roughly 150-kilometre-wide strait between New Guinea and Australia, which today bears his name. It is the first known European voyage through the strait, but the Duyfken had been there a few months earlier without realising that it was a strait.

On 25 October 1616 the Dutch East India Company's ship Eendracht, with Dirk Hartog as skipper, came to an island off Shark Bay that today is called Dirk Hartog Island. It was the second known European landing in Australia and the first on the west coast. Before the ship sailed on on 27 October, Hartog nailed a pewter plate to a post with an inscription about the visit. The plate was found in 1697 by Willem de Vlamingh and is today in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.

On 4 June 1629 the Dutch East India Company's flagship Batavia, on her first voyage, ran aground on a reef at Houtman Abrolhos off Western Australia. Most of those on board made it ashore on small islands, but about 40 drowned. While the commander Francisco Pelsaert sailed in an open boat to Batavia (today Jakarta) for help, Jeronimus Cornelisz took power among the survivors, and over several weeks about 125 people were murdered, among them women and children. When Pelsaert returned with a rescue ship, Cornelisz and several of his men were sentenced and executed.

caption.en: The massacre after the wreck of the Batavia in 1629 on the island called Batavia’s Kerckhof (Batavia’s Graveyard), shown schematically with, among other things, three gallows. Plate by Aart Dircksz Oossaan, after 1680, an amended copy of an illustration in Francisco Pelsaert’s account. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 24 November 1642 Abel Tasman, on a voyage of discovery for the Dutch East India Company, sighted the west coast of Tasmania north of Macquarie Harbour. He called the land Van Diemen's Land after the governor-general of the Dutch East Indies, and today the island bears Tasman's name. On 3 December he formally claimed the land. After a further two days along the east coast he turned east to continue the search for the sought-after southern continent.

In December 1642 Abel Tasman became the first known European to reach New Zealand, and his two ships anchored off the bay that today is called Golden Bay / Mohua, where Māori had lived since at least 1450. Ngāti Tūmatakōkiri went out in a waka (canoe), rammed one of the Dutch boats and killed four sailors. According to archaeological research, the Dutch tried to land at an important cultivation area, which the Māori may have wanted to protect. When the ships left the bay, the ship Zeehaen fired at the waka approaching and hit one man, and Tasman called the place Murderers' Bay.

caption.en: Murderers’ Bay (today Golden Bay / Mohua) on 18 December 1642: the Dutch ships Zeehaen and Heemskerck at anchor with Māori canoes around them. Drawing by Isaack Gilsemans, Abel Tasman’s artist, from the Nationaal Archief. The first European depiction of Māori. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: From 1670 to 1699 the Chamorro people of the Marianas resisted Spanish colonisation. The Spaniards had founded a permanent Jesuit mission at Hagåtña on Guam in 1668, and forced conversions, attempts to destroy ancestral shrines and cultural misunderstandings led in 1670 to a siege of Hagåtña driven by the chief Hurao. After Matå'pang killed the missionary San Vitores in 1672, the Spaniards burned villages, and most of the inhabitants of about 180 villages on Guam were moved to seven places. The Spaniards and the Chamorros on their side prevailed, and by 1699 the population of the northern islands had also been brought to Guam. The violence of the Spaniards and their allies against the Chamorro people has been described as a brutal genocide.

In 1504 Sultan Amara Dunqas founded the Funj Sultanate, an Islamic kingdom in present-day Sudan, with its capital Sennar on the Blue Nile. The kingdom succeeded the Christian Nubian kingdoms and was at its largest at the end of the 17th century. It invited Sufi scholars, which spread Islam in the area. In 1821 the last sultan surrendered to the Turkish-Egyptian conquest.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 1504 as the year the sultanate was founded. Wikidata gives 1505.

summary.en: Mvemba a Nzinga, who took the name Afonso, became king of Kongo in 1509 after a short civil war against his brother. He was a Catholic all his life and worked to make the kingdom Christian. During his time exchange with Portugal grew, both in trade and in religion, but so did the Atlantic slave trade. He ruled from the capital Mbanza Kongo until 1542 or 1543.

text.en: Wikipedia says that Afonso died in 1542 or 1543. Wikidata gives 1543.

summary.en: Between 1593 and 1596 Fort Jesus was built on Mombasa Island to protect the old harbour. The fortress was designed by the Italian architect Giovanni Battista Cairati, but building materials, masonry technique and labour probably came from the Swahili people. It was Portugal's only fort on the Swahili coast. After a siege in 1696–1698, Arabs from Oman took the fort, which largely put an end to the Portuguese presence on the coast.

In 1624 Nzinga took power in Ndongo, a Mbundu kingdom in present-day northern Angola, after her brother. She fought for decades against Portugal, which declared war on Ndongo in 1626. She conquered the neighbouring kingdom of Matamba in 1631–1635 and allied herself with the Dutch. A peace treaty with Portugal was signed in 1656, and she ruled until her death on 17 December 1663. She was born and died in the capital Kabasa. Today she is seen as an important historical figure in Angola.

Emperor Fasilides, who ruled Ethiopia in 1632–1667, chose Gondar in 1636 as his royal camp and made the town the capital of the kingdom. There he had the fortress built that today is called Fasil Ghebbi and is a World Heritage Site. Fasilides restored the Ethiopian Orthodox Church as the state church and banished the Jesuits. The period afterwards is called the Gondarine period.

text.en: Wikipedia says that Fasilides founded Gondar in 1636. Wikidata gives 1635 as the year the town was founded.

summary.en: The Rozvi Empire was a Shona state founded by Changamire Dombo. He defeated the Portuguese and the Mutapa Empire and conquered Butua around 1683. In the 1690s he drove the Portuguese traders out from the plateau. The empire was weakened by drought and civil war and fell in the 1830s under invasions by Nguni peoples during the Mfecane. The last resistance ended in 1866.

text.en: Wikipedia has the empire begin around 1683. Wikidata gives 1660. The sources have few contemporary accounts, because the Portuguese were not let into the kingdom.

summary.en: The Asante king Osei Tutu and his priest Okomfo Anokye united the states of the Asante people around the Golden Stool as a common symbol. In 1701 the Asante army defeated Denkyira and thereby gained access to the coastal trade with the Europeans. The kingdom, with its capital Kumasi, built its wealth on gold, agriculture and the slave trade. It lasted until 1902, when it became part of the British colony of the Gold Coast.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 1701 as the year the kingdom arose. Wikidata gives 1670.

summary.en: On 26 February 1727 King Agaja of Dahomey attacked the port town of Whydah, today Ouidah, and burned the palace. According to reports from the fighting, about 5,000 people were killed and 10,000–11,000 were taken prisoner. The conquest gave Dahomey control of important trade routes for the Atlantic slave trade. Historians disagree about Agaja's reasons.

From 1787 Andrianampoinimerina ruled the kingdom of Imerina on Madagascar from the fortified town of Ambohimanga, today a World Heritage Site. He reunited Imerina after 77 years of civil war and then expanded the kingdom across the highlands. His goal was to unite all of Madagascar, and his son Radama I came far towards that goal during the following two decades.

In 1515 the mosque in Agadez is built, the same year the city comes under the Songhai Empire. The mosque, with a minaret of mud brick, was restored and partly rebuilt in 1844. It still gathers thousands of Muslims for Friday prayers.

In 1520 Sultan Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad makes the city of Harar the new capital of the Adal Sultanate. During the Adal period in the 16th century the city gets a city wall. The old fortified town, Harar Jugol, became a World Heritage Site in 2006.

Around 1655 al-Sa'di, the chronicler of Timbuktu, writes the Tarikh al-Sudan in Arabic. It is the most important source for the history of the Songhai Empire, from the mid-15th century to the Moroccan invasion of 1591, and then tells of Timbuktu under Moroccan rule up to 1655. Al-Sa'di was born in 1594 and in 1646 became chief secretary of the administration in Timbuktu.

In 1662 comes the last widely accepted sighting of a dodo, made on a small islet off Mauritius. The bird was first mentioned by Dutch sailors in 1598. After that it was hunted by sailors and by animals that people had brought to the island, while its habitat was being destroyed. Its extinction was not noticed at once.

text.en: 1662 is the last widely accepted sighting. Wikipedia also mentions a description from 1681, which was long regarded as the last, and the last claimed sighting in 1688. A statistical estimate puts the extinction at around 1693, with a confidence interval of 1688–1715.

summary.en: In 1680 the Pico do Fogo volcano in Cape Verde has a major summit eruption. Ash falls over the whole island and makes the farmland unusable for a time. Many people therefore leave Fogo, among other places for the neighbouring island of Brava.

The Rodrigues solitaire, a flightless bird of the pigeon family found only on the island of Rodrigues east of Madagascar, probably dies out sometime between the 1730s and the 1760s. This coincided with the tortoise trade of 1730–1750: traders burnt the vegetation, hunted the birds and brought in cats and pigs that ate eggs and chicks. When the French astronomer Pingré visited the island in 1761, he saw no solitaires.

text.en: The exact year is unknown. Wikipedia's infobox gives the mid-18th century, and the introduction says the bird was extinct by the late 18th century.

summary.en: On 6 October 1769 James Cook's ship Endeavour sights land off the east coast of the North Island, and shortly afterwards Cook and a group of sailors go ashore at the Tūranganui River in Poverty Bay. His crew is the second known group of Europeans to reach New Zealand, 127 years after Abel Tasman, and Cook is the first known European to go ashore. The first encounters with Māori turned violent, and several Māori were killed. Further south, at Anaura Bay and Tolaga Bay, the encounters were more peaceful, and the Tahitian Tupaia interpreted.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on Cook's first voyage says that Cook went ashore on 7 October and that four or five Māori died in the first two days. Wikipedia's article on Gisborne gives 9 October and says that nine Māori were killed or wounded over four days. The sources do not explain the difference. Among the first to be killed was Te Maro, who since 2019 has been honoured with a memorial on the hill Titirangi.

summary.en: On 3 July 1721 the Dano-Norwegian priest Hans Egede settled on the Island of Hope in Godthåb Fjord with his family and other colonists. He wanted to do missionary work and to search for descendants of the Norse settlers. This is regarded as the beginning of the Dano-Norwegian colonisation of Greenland.

In 1728 the first colony was moved from Kangeq to the mainland, and the colony of Godthåb was founded. It is today's capital, Nuuk. Hans Egede's stone house from 1728 is the oldest surviving building in Greenland.

In 1776 the state-owned company Den Kongelige Grønlandske Handel (KGH, the Royal Greenland Trade) was given the sole right to trade with Greenland, a monopoly that lasted until 1950. In practice KGH was the administration of the colony. The company bought seal oil, fish and skins from Greenlandic hunters and sold European goods in Greenland.

text.en: The sources agree on the monopoly in 1776, but not on when the company was founded: Lex (the article on KGH) and SNL give 1776, while Lex's overview and Wikipedia give 1774.

summary.en: Malmö surrenders in April 1536, and when the Catholic Church is overthrown in Denmark, the archdiocese of Lund comes to an end. Lund's power had rested on the Church. After the Reformation, all the monasteries and churches in the town except the cathedral and two others were demolished, and Lund became an ordinary Danish provincial town.

After the Swedish army has crossed the frozen belts, peace is concluded at Roskilde. Denmark cedes all its land east of the Øresund to Sweden, that is Scania with Bornholm, Halland and Blekinge, and the island of Ven. Norway cedes the provinces of Bohus and Trondheim.

text.en: Den Store Danske and Nordisk familjebok give 26 February 1658. English Wikipedia gives 26 February in the old (Julian) calendar, that is 8 March in the Gregorian. Wikidata gives 28 February.

summary.en: After the conquest, the Swedish state makes Scania Swedish. Swedish law, the Swedish church ordinance and Swedish as the language of church, school and courts are introduced, and Lund University trains priests. At first the process was slow, but after the Scanian War the Swedification was pushed hard.

text.en: Swedish Wikipedia dates the Swedification to 1658–1719, with Swedish law in the 1680s and the Swedish church ordinance in 1686. Lex.dk (danmarkshistorien.dk) says that an agreement in 1662 at first prevented any real Swedification, and that the real Swedification began after the end of the war in 1679, with a campaign after 1681. Nordisk familjebok says that the Swedification was complete by the end of the Great Northern War in 1720.

summary.en: Representatives of the nobility, clergy, burghers and peasants of Scania, Blekinge and Halland gather in Malmö and swear allegiance to Charles X Gustav. The king was not there in person; an empty chair stood in his place.

text.en: The date and place come only from English Wikipedia. Nordisk familjebok mentions the oath of allegiance and that much of the nobility was reluctant to take it, but gives no date or place.

summary.en: The peace ends the second Karl Gustav war between Denmark and Sweden, 1658–1660. Denmark–Norway keeps Bornholm and gets back the province of Trondheim, but Sweden keeps Scania, Halland, Blekinge and Bohuslän. With this, Scania was finally separated from Denmark.

text.en: Den Store Danske and Wikidata give 27 May 1660. Den Store Danske does not say which calendar the date follows, and Wikidata marks it as Gregorian.

summary.en: The charter of Lund University is issued. For Sweden, a university in Scania was an important tool for making the conquered provinces Swedish, not least by training priests. The university was inaugurated in 1668.

text.en: Founded on 19 December 1666 and inaugurated on 28 January 1668 according to Nordisk familjebok. Den Store Danske gives the same founding date and says only that the university was inaugurated in 1668.

summary.en: Denmark–Norway tries to win back the Scanian lands. In the summer of 1676 a Danish army lands at Råå and quickly takes Helsingborg, Landskrona and Kristianstad, but is defeated at Lund in December. Denmark wins control of the sea, but the peace of 1679, which France in effect dictated, restores the borders of 1660.

text.en: The war was fought in several places. The point shows Scania, where the fighting over the province took place. The sources do not name a single place where the war began.

summary.en: Charles XI's Swedish army crosses the frozen Lödde river by night without being discovered and meets the Danish army under Christian V on the heights north of Lund. The Swedes win, and what is left of the Danish army withdraws to Landskrona. It became the largest land battle of the Scanian War.

text.en: Den Store Danske and Nordisk familjebok give 4 December 1676. Wikidata marks the date as Julian. The sources give different sizes for the armies.

summary.en: During the Scanian War, Scanian friskyttar (“free marksmen”) in Danish service wage a guerrilla war against the Swedish army, and outright robber bands also roamed the land. The Swedes called them all snapphanes, and those who were captured were harshly punished. At the end of the war, at least 500 friskyttar were transferred to Denmark.

text.en: Snapphane was the Swedes' term of abuse. Nordisk familjebok distinguishes between the organised friskyttar and outright robber bands. In Denmark they were called gønger, after the Göinge districts on the border.

summary.en: The peace ends the Scanian War after Dutch and French mediation. Everything Denmark had conquered is handed back, and the terms of the Treaty of Copenhagen of 1660 apply again.

text.en: Den Store Danske and Wikidata give 26 September 1679. English Wikipedia gives 16 September in the old calendar and 26 September in the new.

summary.en: The Scanian governor-generalship comes to an end, and Scania is governed like other Swedish provinces through two counties, Malmöhus County and Kristianstad County. The county borders were adjusted in 1720.

text.en: Nordisk familjebok and Store norske leksikon give 1719. According to Swedish Wikipedia, the counties existed earlier: Kristianstad County got a governor in 1658, and Malmöhus County was formed in 1669. The governor-generalship had also ended once in 1669 and been revived in 1676. In 1719 it ended for good.

summary.en: The Jesuit Francis Xavier reached Japan on 27 July 1549 and went ashore at Kagoshima on Kyushu on 15 August. He worked in Japan for more than two years, among other places in Yamaguchi, and Christian congregations were formed in Hirado, Yamaguchi and Bungo. The daimyo of Satsuma first received him kindly but the following year forbade his subjects to become Christians, on pain of death.

In 1565 Andrés de Urdaneta found the return route across the Pacific from the Philippines to Mexico, and Spanish galleons began sailing between Manila and Acapulco. They mainly carried Chinese silk and porcelain east in exchange for silver from the Americas. One or two ships sailed each way every year. The trade ended in 1815.

The oldest surviving edition of the novel Journey to the West was printed in 1592 in Nanjing. It is a free, fantastic account of the monk Xuanzang's journey to India in the 7th century to fetch Buddhist scriptures, with the monkey Sun Wukong as one of his disciples. The novel is traditionally attributed to Wu Cheng'en, but who wrote it is disputed.

At the request of the Wanli Emperor, a large world map, Kunyu Wanguo Quantu, was printed in Beijing in 1602. It was made by the Jesuit Matteo Ricci together with the Chinese collaborators Zhong Wentao and Li Zhizao. It is the first map in Chinese to show the Americas, and the oldest known Chinese world map based on European cartography. China lies at the centre.

In 1603 Izumo no Okuni, a former shrine maiden, began performing with a troupe of women on a simple stage in the dry bed of the Kamo River in Kyoto. This is regarded as the beginning of kabuki. In 1629 women were banned from performing kabuki, and since then all roles have been played by men.

In 1604 Guru Arjan, the fifth Sikh Guru, placed a copy of the holy scripture Adi Granth in the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar. The brick temple itself had been completed in 1589. Today it is called the Golden Temple.

In May 1637 Song Yingxing's encyclopedia of technology, the Tiangong Kaiwu, was published with money from his patron Tu Shaokui. The book describes, among other things, farming, boats, silk and cotton making, metalwork and gunpowder. Under the Qing dynasty the book became very rare in China.

In 1641 the Dutch trading post was moved from Hirado to Dejima, an artificial island in Nagasaki that the shogun Iemitsu had ordered built from 1634. During Japan's isolation, Dejima was for about 220 years the main channel for foreign trade and cultural exchange, and the Dutch were the only Westerners allowed to trade with Japan. The monopoly ended in 1858.

According to tradition, the tenth Sikh Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, gathered his followers at Anandpur Sahib at the Vaisakhi festival on 13 April 1699. Five men who were ready to give their lives became the first members of the Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs. He initiated them with amrit, water and sugar stirred with a double-edged sword, and then had himself initiated by them.

text.en: The year 1699 became widely accepted only through a work from the late 19th century. Early Sikh sources from the 18th century give years between 1695 and 1698, and one source gives 1689.

summary.en: On 16 December 1707 Mount Fuji began to erupt, 49 days after the great Hōei earthquake. The ash reached Edo, today's Tokyo, almost 100 kilometres away, where it lay several centimetres thick. The eruption is regarded as the worst ash-fall disaster in Japanese history. Crop failure led to famine, and in 1708 heavy rain caused avalanches of ash and mud. It is Fuji's latest eruption.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the eruption says it ended on 24 February 1708. The article on Mount Fuji says around 1 January 1708.

summary.en: The Rajput king Sawai Jai Singh, founder of Jaipur, had an observatory built with nineteen stone instruments for measuring time and following the heavenly bodies. He wanted better astronomical tables than those that existed. Several instruments were finished by 1728 and the site in 1734. It has the world's largest gnomon sundial, about 27 metres high. It became a World Heritage Site in 2010.

In 1782–1788 Japan was struck by famine, worst in Tōhoku in northeastern Honshu. The eruption of Mount Asama in 1783 and cold weather destroyed the harvests, and the shogunate's policies had made farmers dependent on rice and emptied the emergency food stores. The Hirosaki domain lost almost half its population, counting those who fled. Between 1780 and 1786 Japan's population fell by more than 920,000 people through famine and disease.

The Hatata ("inquiry" in Ge'ez) are two philosophical treatises on ethics and reason from what is today Ethiopia. The first was written by Zara Yaqob, according to the text in 1668, and the second some years later by his pupil Walda Heywat. Zara Yaqob writes that he fled from Aksum and lived for two years in a cave.

text.en: Who wrote the Hatata is disputed. In 1920 Carlo Conti Rossini claimed that the Italian priest Giusto da Urbino wrote the texts himself, and the scholar Anaïs Wion shares that view. Others, among them Claude Sumner and Getatchew Haile, and the translators of the 2023 edition, hold that the authors were Ethiopians.

summary.en: The bluebuck, an antelope found only in the southwestern Cape, was hunted to extinction by European settlers. The last animal was shot in 1799 or 1800, probably in the area around Swellendam. It is the first historically recorded case of a large African mammal species becoming extinct.
